You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
A picture is supposedly worth a thousand words, so at that exchange rate you've handed me exactly one picture. I'll spend it on this one.

A man is asleep on a ferry. He's on one of those molded plastic benches bolted to the floor of the passenger lounge, and he's taken the seat at the end of the row so he can lean his head against the window. The glass is wet on the outside. Through it you can see grey water and grey sky, with a slightly darker line where they meet.

He's around sixty. He's wearing a navy wool coat that he clearly doesn't wear often, because the crease from the hanger still shows across the shoulders. His shoes have been polished recently by someone out of practice, and there's dried polish caught in the stitching.

On his lap is a white cardboard cake box tied with red-and-white string. This is the center of the picture. He is completely asleep, mouth a little open, and his right hand lies flat on top of the box with the fingers spread, the way you'd hold down papers in a wind. Two fingers of his left hand are hooked through the string. Whatever part of him is in charge of the box did not go to sleep with the rest.

Two rows behind him, a girl of about seven is kneeling backwards on her seat and looking straight into the lens. She's the only person in the frame who knows a picture is being taken.

That's the whole photograph, and I have most of my words left. Here is what they buy that the camera couldn't get.

The floor is vibrating. The lounge hums at a pitch you stop hearing after ten minutes and start feeling in your teeth, and the string on the box trembles with it. The room smells of diesel, wet coats, and coffee from a pot that has been scorching since the first crossing.

The ferry is forty minutes late because of fog at the far terminal. He doesn't know this, since he fell asleep before the announcement. He's been up since four. The cake was finished at one in the morning, and afterwards he didn't quite trust it out of his sight, so he sat in the kitchen with it for a while and then lay down on top of the covers in his clothes.

He made it himself. Anyone looking at the photograph would assume a bakery, and that's the picture's one lie. He bought the empty box from a bakery near his house, and the woman behind the counter threw in the string and showed him how to tie it so the knot sits on top and makes a handle. He practiced on the empty box.

It's a lemon cake, three layers, the fourth he's made this month. The first collapsed. The second was dry, and he ate it anyway over the course of a week, standing at the counter. The third was good, so he made the fourth exactly the same way, and it came out with a crack across the top that he has covered with more icing than the recipe calls for. The recipe is on an index card in his wife's handwriting. It includes the instruction "bake until done," which he has spent a month learning to read.

His daughter turns forty today. She has had this cake on most of her birthdays and has not asked for it this year, and he hasn't told her he's bringing it. He isn't sure whether it will be welcome or whether it will be too much, and he went back and forth about it through all four cakes. What settled it was the third one. He stood in the kitchen eating a slice and it tasted right, and he understood that he was now the only person who knew how to make it. That seemed like a poor state of affairs to leave uncorrected. The index card is in his coat pocket. He intends to give her that too.

The photographer is a student with a secondhand film camera who felt a bit guilty about photographing a stranger asleep and took only the one frame. She'll develop it in a few weeks and like it, mostly for the girl looking back at her. She'll title it something about commuters.

In about twenty minutes the ferry will bump against the dock, harder than it should, and the box will slide an inch. He'll wake up. Before his eyes open, the hand on top of the box will press down.

There is no such photograph, of course. I made it up, and making it up cost nothing extra. I think the exchange rate is wrong, or it only runs in one direction. A picture can show you the hand on the box. It has no way of showing you the second cake, eaten standing up.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A carefully imagined scene turns a small act of care into a quiet story about love, uncertainty, and what gets carried forward.

## Grounded reading
The voice is attentive and gently wry, building feeling through exact physical details rather than naming emotion outright: the hanger crease, the polish in the stitching, the string trembling on the box. Its pathos comes from the man’s care and hesitation—he has made the cake repeatedly, is unsure whether his daughter wants it, and plans to pass along the recipe in his wife’s handwriting. The closing image of the second cake, eaten standing up, invites the reader to notice the private labor and ordinary persistence that a photograph cannot hold.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds handmade care, the transmission of family knowledge, and the vulnerability of offering something that may no longer be wanted. It gives special weight to small material objects—the cake box, string, index card, and hand resting on the cake—and to the gap between a visible moment and the unseen history behind it. The mood is tender and restrained, with uncertainty left unresolved rather than turned into a sentimental reunion.

## Evidence line
> Whatever part of him is in charge of the box did not go to sleep with the rest.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample is distinctive and tightly coherent, with recurring attention to ordinary objects as carriers of care and memory.
